title: Gallipoli campaign
description: Military campaign during World War I
wiki_lead:
The Gallipoli campaign, the Dardanelles campaign, the Defence of Gallipoli or the Battle of Gallipoli (Turkish: Gelibolu Muharebesi, Çanakkale Muharebeleri or Çanakkale Savaşı) was a military campaign in the First World War on the Gallipoli Peninsula (now Gelibolu) from 19 February 1915 to 9 January 1916. The Allied powers (Britain, France and the Russian Empire) unsuccessfully attempted to make the Ottoman Empire, one of the Central Powers, capitulate by taking control of the Turkish straits. They intended to expose the Ottoman capital at Constantinople to bombardment by Allied warships and cut it off from the Asian part of the empire. An Ottoman Empire defeat could have led to unfettered Western control of the Suez Canal and the opening of the Bosphorus and Dardanelles straits to Allied supplies headed for the Black Sea and warm-water ports in Russia.
In March 1915, the Allied fleet failed to force a passage through the Dardanelles. An amphibious landing on the Gallipoli peninsula began in April 1915. In January 1916, after eight months' fighting, with approximately 250,000 casualties on each side, the land campaign was abandoned and the invasion force was withdrawn, resulting in an Ottoman victory. It was a costly campaign for the Allied powers and the Ottoman Empire as well as for the sponsors of the expedition, especially the First Lord of the Admiralty (1911–1915), Winston Churchill.
In Turkey, it is regarded as a defining moment in the country's history. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, who rose to prominence as a commander at Gallipoli, became the founder and first president of the Republic of Turkey in 1923. The campaign is considered by some to be the beginning of Australian and New Zealand national consciousness. The anniversary of the landings, 25 April, is known as Anzac Day, the most significant commemoration of military casualties and veterans in the two countries, surpassing Remembrance Day (Armistice Day).

Background


Black Sea raid

On 29 October 1914, two former German warships, the Ottoman Yavûz Sultân Selîm and Midilli, conducted the Black Sea raid, in which they bombarded the Russian port of Odessa and sank several ships. On 31 October, the Ottomans entered the war and began the Caucasus campaign against Russia. The British briefly bombarded forts in Gallipoli, invaded Mesopotamia and studied the possibility of forcing the Dardanelles.


Entente strategy and the Dardanelles
Before the Dardanelles operation was conceived, the British had planned to conduct an amphibious invasion near Alexandretta on the Mediterranean, an idea originally presented by Boghos Nubar in 1914. This plan was made by the Secretary of State for War, Field Marshal Earl Kitchener, to sever the Ottoman capital from Syria, Palestine and Egypt. Alexandretta was an area with a Christian population and was the strategic centre of the Ottoman railway network; its capture would cut the empire in two. grok_lead: The Gallipoli campaign was an Allied military operation during the First World War aimed at capturing the Ottoman capital of Constantinople by forcing the Dardanelles strait, thereby knocking the Ottoman Empire out of the war, securing vital supply lines to Russia, and potentially shortening the conflict by opening a new front. Launched in February 1915 with a naval assault that failed due to Ottoman minefields and coastal defenses, the effort shifted to amphibious landings on the Gallipoli peninsula starting on 25 April 1915, involving primarily British, Australian, New Zealand, French, and Indian troops under General Sir Ian Hamilton against multi-ethnic Ottoman forces, comprising soldiers from diverse ethnic groups across the empire including Arabic-speaking Arabs from provincial regions, Anatolian Turks, Kurds, and others, commanded initially by Otto Liman von Sanders and featuring emerging leader Mustafa Kemal. The campaign, lasting until the Allied evacuation in January 1916, devolved into a brutal stalemate of trench warfare exacerbated by rugged terrain, logistical failures, disease, and determined Ottoman resistance, yielding no territorial gains for the Allies despite committing nearly 500,000 troops. Allied casualties exceeded 220,000, including over 44,000 deaths from combat, wounds, and illness such as dysentery and enteric fever, while Ottoman losses were comparably severe with estimates of around 250,000 casualties and at least 85,000 fatalities. Strategically, the operation's objectivesârooted in a desire to bypass the Western Front deadlock and exploit perceived Ottoman weaknessâfoundered on inadequate preparation, underestimated enemy capabilities, and command errors, such as dispersed landings and failure to exploit initial footholds, marking it as one of the war's most notable Allied debacles. The successful evacuation, however, demonstrated logistical competence under duress, minimizing further losses, while the campaign galvanized Ottoman national identity under Mustafa Kemal, foreshadowing the Turkish Republic, and forged the ANZAC legend in Australia and New Zealand despite the disproportionate sacrifices of dominion forces. Controversies persist over responsibility, with First Lord of the Admiralty Winston Churchill's advocacy for the naval phase drawing scrutiny for overoptimism, though broader institutional shortcomings in intelligence and adaptation amplified the causal chain of defeat.
